doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Reading Monk's music in the studio, and Monk at Blue Note
summary: Monk's tricky tunes needed rehearsal, and Donaldson explains why audiences and big companies were not ready for Monk.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: The date with Monk, then. I’ve read a quote from you that you hadn’t worked with Monk before that; that you had to go in and basically read the music down...
Yeah, try to.
Maybe there was a rehearsal before.
Try to read it. He didn’t write it out like he wanted it played. You had to rehearse it a couple of times. But it ended up fine.
There were a couple of tricky tunes on that session.
Yes, sir.
“Skippy” for one.
“Skippy” is tough. “Carolina Moon” is tough. Tough tune.
How did the session go? He’d present the tune, you’d run through it a few times, and then...
And then we recorded it.
How did he express his intentions? Would he be singing it to you?
He played it on the piano, you know...
Had you known Monk before that?
Yes, I knew him.
Because he spent a lot of time at Minton’s, I would think, among other places...
Not at Minton’s. He was at Blue Note. Every time I went down there, Monk and his wife would be down there, at the company, down there in back of Bloomingdale’s. They’d be down there all the time.
What was the office like?
Wasn’t nothing but just a little place. Wasn’t really an office.
Were you a fan of Monk’s compositions, of his music, his musicianship?

Not really. I couldn’t use them on my job, because if I played them, I’d be fired. See, back then people hadn’t...they wasn’t compatible with Monk. It took a long time before they got compatible with Monk.
How so?
Well, they wouldn’t buy his records.
Oh, you mean before people got used to his music and the sound of it.
Yes. And the big companies wouldn’t record him. Like Capitol, Columbia, even Savoy—they wouldn’t record him.
No, he was on Blue Note, then he went to Prestige...
Prestige, right.
